summary: This standards-track memo defines metrics for judging whether a network keeps packets in order, starting with a reordered singleton and building measures of how much, how often and how far apart reordering happens. It includes a metric aimed at the effect on TCP. It was later updated by RFC 6248.

eli5.summary: Imagine numbered cards arriving shuffled. This defines ways to measure how shuffled they are, so people can describe a network's behavior with numbers.

subtitle: A toolkit of measurements for answering how badly, how often and how far apart a network shuffles packets.

tldr.problem: IP does not guarantee that packets arrive in the order they were sent, and different applications are hurt by reordering in different ways, so there was no agreed way to say how reordered a path is.
tldr.mechanism: Each packet carries a source sequence number. The receiver keeps a never-decreasing NextExp value and calls any packet below it reordered. Sample metrics then count and size the reordering by position, time, bytes, spacing and a TCP-oriented n-reordering measure.
tldr.outcome: The memo gives network operators and receiver designers a common vocabulary and registered metric names. It was later updated by RFC 6248.

facts.label: Core test
facts.value: Reordered if s is less than NextExp

today: RFC 4737 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 6248, so read the two together.

sections.title: Why Measure Packet Order
sections.content:
IP has no mechanism to ensure packet delivery or sequencing, so higher layers must be ready to cope with both loss and reordering. This memo defines reordering metrics: ways to evaluate, packet by packet, whether a network kept order.

Reordering is detected by comparing arrival order with a non-reversing reference value. A packet whose sequence number is smaller than its predecessors is called reordered. If packets numbered 1, 2, 4, 5, 3 arrive in that order, packet 3 is the reordered one. The memo focuses on these late packets rather than on the premature ones (4 and 5), because that keeps the metric independent of the packet loss metric.

The RFC lists causes: several paths with different transfer times, devices with multiple processors serving one port, layer-2 retransmission on error-prone links, and buffers that are not served in arrival order. Steady-state reordering shows up as a sizeable fraction of packets, while transient reordering, such as from temporary routing loops, shows up as long in-order stretches with occasional bursts.

Every reordering metric must be reported together with its measurement context: the packet type and addresses, and the stream parameters of the sending discipline, including packet size. Without that context reordering is not well defined.
sections.eli5: If you mail numbered postcards, some may arrive in the wrong order because they took different roads. This RFC is about counting how mixed up they got, and it insists you also write down how you sent them.

sections.title: The Reordered Singleton
sections.content:
The basic building block is a singleton metric named Type-P-Reordered. The sender applies a strictly increasing identifier s to each packet, and the receiver stores NextExp, the next expected sequence number.

When a packet with sequence number s arrives, it is in-order if s is greater than or equal to NextExp, and NextExp becomes s + 1. If s is smaller than NextExp the packet is reordered and NextExp does not change. Because NextExp cannot decrease, it is a non-reversing criterion. The first packet to arrive is in-order by definition.

An in-order packet with s greater than NextExp marks a sequence discontinuity of size s - NextExp, the number of packets currently missing, whether lost or merely late. Only if the missing packets later arrive is it a reordering discontinuity.

Duplicates MUST be noted and only the first copy is analysed, since later copies would otherwise be declared reordered. Time and payload bytes can serve as alternative dimensions, but the memo notes that discontinuities are hard to define there, so they are mainly used to describe the extent of reordering.
sections.eli5: Keep a note of the next card number you expect. A card with a number lower than that note is late. A card that jumps ahead leaves a hole that may be filled in later.

sections.title: Sample Metrics: Ratio, Extent, Time and Bytes
sections.content:
The sample metrics apply to a stream of K packets sent, of which L are received (duplicates removed, so L is at most K). A waiting time dT acts as the threshold for declaring a packet lost.

  • Reordered Packet Ratio (Type-P-Reordered-Ratio-Stream): the count of reordered packets divided by L. If it is zero, no further reordering metrics need be examined for that sample.
  • Reordering Extent (Type-P-Packet-Reordering-Extent-Stream): for a reordered packet at arrival index i, the extent e is i - j for the smallest j where the packet at j has a larger sequence number. It is roughly the number of packets a receiver must hold while waiting, though it can overestimate the storage needed.
  • Late Time Offset (Type-P-Packet-Late-Time-Stream): the arrival time of the reordered packet minus the arrival time of the earliest packet with a larger sequence number. It shows how much buffer time, such as in a de-jitter buffer, is needed.
  • Byte Offset (Type-P-Packet-Byte-Offset-Stream): the sum of payload sizes of packets that arrived earlier but carry a greater sequence number, which approximates buffer space in bytes.

Results can be summarised as histograms or as a cumulative distribution function, which helps tune receiver buffers.
sections.eli5: You can ask how many cards were late, how many cards you had to hold while waiting, how long you waited, and how much table space the held cards took up.

sections.title: Gaps and Reordering-Free Runs
sections.content:
Two metrics describe how reordering events are spaced. Every reordered packet is tied to a reordering discontinuity, the in-order packet at the smallest arrival index that carries a larger sequence number. The Reordering Gap is the distance, in arrival positions, between successive discontinuities, and it may also be given in time as GapTime. If there is no earlier discontinuity the gap is 0.

The Reordering-Free Run metric counts consecutive in-order packets between reordered packets, and a run can have length zero. The memo keeps four counters: x (number of runs, also the number of reordered packets), a (in-order packets), p (all packets) and q (the sum of the squares of the run lengths). The percent in-order is 100*a/p and the average run length is a/x. Comparing q/a with a/x shows how much run lengths vary.

For 36 packets with 3 runs, equal runs of 11 give a variability ratio of 1.0, while runs of 1, 1 and 31 give a ratio of 2.65. Long runs mean order was kept for a while, and short runs mean frequent or multi-packet reordering.
sections.eli5: The gap tells you how far apart two mix-ups happened. A run tells you how many cards in a row came in the right order before the next mix-up.

sections.title: n-Reordering for TCP
sections.content:
Section 5 adds a metric aimed at how reordering affects TCP: Type-P-Packet-n-Reordering-Stream. A received packet is n-reordered if every one of the n packets that arrived immediately before it has a larger sequence number. A packet that is n-reordered is also n'-reordered for any smaller positive n'. The degree of n-reordering of a sample is the number of n-reordered packets divided by the number received.

The point is to estimate whether reordering would push a sender past its duplicate-ACK threshold and trigger Fast Retransmit. That threshold is 3 for TCP according to the RFC, and also the default for SCTP and for DCCP with TCP-like congestion control. A NewReno sender facing 3-reordering would retransmit one packet and halve its congestion window. If a path shows no more than 5-reordering, the memo says a threshold of 6 may avoid unnecessary retransmissions.

To infer anything about TCP, the test stream MUST closely resemble the TCP sender of interest. The memo also warns that n-reordering cannot predict the exact number of needless retransmissions, since both timing and position matter. It is not defined for every reordered packet: in the arrival order 1,2,3,7,8,9,4,5,6, packets 4, 5 and 6 are reordered but only packet 4 is n-reordered, with n=3.
sections.eli5: TCP gets nervous when it sees a few later cards arrive first and may ask for a resend that was not needed. This measure counts how often that nervous point would be reached.

sections.title: Measurement and Implementation Issues
sections.content:
Results depend on the spacing of test packets: packets sent rarely, for example one per 10 seconds, are unlikely to be reordered. The RFC RECOMMENDS using the same sending pattern as the application of interest and requires reporting the packet generation method and all stream parameters. To draw conclusions about TCP applications, TCP-like streams as in RFC 3148 are REQUIRED. For real-time applications, periodic streams as in RFC 3432 are RECOMMENDED. Poisson streams from RFC 2330 are acceptable for the Section 3 and 4 metrics, but not for inferences about those application categories.

Varying packet lengths can reveal parallel processing; a line-speed burst of the longest packets followed by the shortest is given as an effective pattern. Streams sent at the link speed limit MUST have limited duration, and packet loss should be read as a sign of congestion that suspends testing.

Loss alone does not cause later packets to be declared reordered. Finite sequence numbers can roll over, after which all packets would look reordered, so the memo suggests detecting large jumps and using extended precision. Storage can be limited by keeping only discontinuity information, a sliding history window, or a list of missing packet numbers for duplicate detection. Nested or overlapping events make extents and gaps tricky. The metrics were designed for active measurement but can also be applied passively.
sections.eli5: How you send the test packets changes what you find. So send them the way the real program would, and always say how you did it.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Section 7 walks through four arrival orders with tables of delay, IPDV, byte offset and late time.

  • One packet late: arrival order 1,2,3,5,6,7,8,4,9,10. Packet 4 has extent 4, a late time of 62 ms and, with 100-byte payloads, a byte offset of 400. It is 4-reordered.
  • Two packets late: arrival order 1,2,3,4,7,5,6,8,9,10. Packets 5 and 6 share one reordering discontinuity at packet 7. Packet 6 has extent 2 although only one packet needs storing, which shows how extent can overestimate. Packet 5 is 1-reordered but packet 6 is not n-reordered.
  • Three packets late: arrival order 1,2,3,7,8,9,10,4,5,6,11. All three map to the discontinuity at packet 7, and only packet 4 is n-reordered.
  • Two discontinuities: arrival order 1,2,3,6,7,4,5,8,9,10,12,13,11,14,15,16. The gap is 7, and the reordering-free runs have lengths 5, 0 and 5.

The last example shows the difference between the two multi-event metrics: gaps measure distance between discontinuities, while runs measure distance between reordered packets.
sections.eli5: The examples are like a teacher showing a few shuffled lists and working out each score by hand, so you can check you counted the same way.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
The metrics need a stream of packets from a source to a destination, so the method could be abused for denial-of-service attacks on the endpoints or intervening networks. The RFC advises bilateral or multilateral agreements on timing, size and frequency of sampling, and says excess use may lead to packets being discarded.

Active measurement uses generated packets and does not threaten user data confidentiality. Passive measurement must restrict itself to the headers of interest, and stored payloads MUST be kept safe and confidential; a hash is usually enough for comparing payloads. Someone who can identify the test packets could treat them differently, or inject extra packets that would be seen as duplicates and spoil the result. The RFC points to the OWAMP documents, RFC 3763 and RFC 4656, for resistance to interference.

IANA registered the metrics in the IPPM metrics registry, using identities numbered 34 through 45, from ietfReorderedSingleton to ietfnReordering.
sections.eli5: Sending lots of test packets could annoy or overload someone, so agree first. And keep any peeked-at mail private.
